source_title: Autumn Budget 2026: LGA briefing - Local Government Association
source_excerpt:
A summary of the key announcements for councils in the 2026 Autumn Budget and the LGA's initial view.
This briefing provides a summary of the key announcements in the 2026 Autumn Budget relevant to local government. The full set of documents is available on the Treasury website .
The LGA has published a media statement responding to the announcements .
The Government recognises that councils are central to achieving good growth and rewiring the state, with commitments towards greater fiscal devolution to local areas and prevention and early intervention. However, these ambitions cannot be achieved if council finances remain fragile and reliant on emergency bailout agreements. The full value of local government will only be unleashed if local authorities are empowered and financially sustainable alongside strategic authorities.
Devolution: We welcome the Government’s commitment to greater fiscal devolution across England. The UK is one of the most fiscally centralised countries in the developed world so plans for greater fiscal devolution are encouraging. However, genuine devolution must provide councils as well as mayors and strategic authorities, with the funding, powers and flexibility to respond to local priorities and deliver for residents.
Fiscal devolution: Given the scale of the financial challenge faced by councils and the Government’s overall ambitions for fiscal devolution it is disappointing that the fiscal devolution offer to councils is no more than the retention of an additional 20 per cent of business rates, in lieu of existing grants, in three years’ time. The sector faces a £7 billion funding gap by 2028/29 compared 2025/26, and nearly one in three (30 per cent) councils expect to need Exceptional Financial Support in 2028/29. The measures set out in the Budget will not address this situation.
Reducing the burden on councils : It is also disappointing that the Budget makes no reference to the Government’s commitment to look at ways to reduce burdens on local authorities created by statutory duties, while ensuring that essential services communities rely on are maintained. Given the financial pressures faced by the sector and the lack of additional financial support provided in the Budget we urge Government to take forward this commitment at pace.
A programme of reform : While this Budget does little to address the immediate challenges faced by councils, we do recognise that the Government has committed to a longer-term programme of reform to support the financial sustainability to councils. In this context it is vital that Government uses the Rewiring the State Delivery Plan and the forthcoming 10-Year Plan to introduce measures to ensure that councils are empowered, financially sustainable, and at the placed at the heart of ongoing reform. Government must also deliver its proposed reforms to the highest cost services as quickly as possible.
Devolution and Local Government Reorganisation: The LGA will continue to support areas through local government reorganisation and the establishment of Strategic and Foundational Authorities, including those announced today. Councils have already committed significant time, capacity and resources to this process, and all costs must be fully funded. Councils cannot be expected to bear the financial and staffing consequences of decisions beyond their control. We welcome government’s flexible approach and open discussions with local leaders about structures.
Children’s social care: It is disappointing the Budget does not announce any funding for children’s social care. Children’s social care remains under significant financial pressure. Long-term funding must reflect rising demand and costs, workforce pressures and the impact of local government reorganisation.
SEND: Supporting the growing number of children and young people with SEND is one of councils’ biggest challenges. While councils welcomed the 90 per cent write-off previously announced, it is disappointing that there is no clarity in the Budget on how DSG deficits accruing in 2026/27 and 2027/28 will be addressed. Government must also clarify residual liabilities faced by councils. We will work with parliamentarians on the forthcoming legislation to deliver a SEND system that delivers for all.
Prevention: We welcome the Government’s recognition of the importance of prevention and early intervention through the new Preventative Departmental Expenditure Limits (PDEL). Councils are uniquely placed to drive prevention across services and places, and the LGA looks forward working through the detail with Government in order to strengthen the evidence base for prevention. Funding for prevention needs to be sufficient to adequately fund preventative services but this alone will not be enough to secure the financial sustainability of councils given the funding gap facing local government.
Adult social care and winter pressures: While we welcome the additional £190 million for the NHS to help address winter pressures, these are a system-wide challenge and will require greater investment. It is therefore disappointing that there is no corresponding funding for adult social care, which plays a vital role in preventing hospital admissions, supporting timely discharge and helping people live independently. The Casey Commission – now working to an accelerated timetable that was welcomed by the LGA – provides an opportunity to build a lasting settlement for care and support. Reform must start from a recognition of the significant immediate pressures facing councils and the people and communities they serve, and any lasting settlement must be co-produced and locally led, with councils remaining central to its delivery.
Housing: We welcome the additional £1.5 billion announced for social and affordable housing, bringing funding through the Social and Affordable Homes Programme up to £40 billion over the next ten years. However, this is only part of what is needed to meet councils’ ambition. We want the Government to go further to accelerate the delivery of social rented homes, alongside wider reforms to planning, regulation and land supply that will enable more homes of all tenures to be built.
Homelessness: As set out in the LGA’s Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy Position Statement 2026 , councils need long-term funding certainty and a stronger focus on prevention to deliver sustainable reductions in homelessness and rough sleeping. Additionally, it is disappointing that there was no announcement around Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rates being uprated to the 30th percentile of local rents, nor that temporary accommodation reimbursement rules would be uprated to 90 per cent of the prevailing LHA rates. Councils are facing immense financial pressures – with council expenditure on temporary accommodation increasing by a massive 1077 per cent in real terms between 2011/12 and 2024/25.
Growth: The LGA welcomes the Good Growth Fund and recognition that growth funding must reach more places. As set out in the LGA’s A force for growth report , funding should be long-term and flexible, with sufficient revenue support to build capacity in every area, regardless of devolution status.

The Budget confirms that day-to-day departmental spending will continue to grow overall in real terms over the forecast period, but it will be more gradual, controlled and targeted. The 10 Year Plan will set out the government’s long-term vision and priorities ahead of the next spending review. The next spending review will take place in 2027. As the government continues to target investment into the country’s top priorities, it is not necessarily the case that all departments will see real terms increases at the next spending review. (Page 31, paragraph 2.3)

The Government intends for local and regional government to retain 100 per cent of business rates income before the end of the decade in place of grants from central government, with the share retained by local authorities increasing to at least 70 per cent. This process will begin with MSAs receiving a 20 per cent share of business rates from April 2027. The government will seek views from the sector on how best to achieve 100 per cent business rates retention. (Pages 65 - 66, paragraph 4.66)
Increased business rates retention should be accompanied by a robust equalisation mechanism with regular resets that strikes the balance between incentivising local authorities to pursue growth and the need to recognise the differing resource raising capacity of different places. Likewise, there must be measures in place to protect councils’ income from economic shocks, alongside an efficient, effective and transparent appeals process that provides councils with as much certainty on income as possible.
The LGA and local authorities worked effectively with MHCLG on the design of 100 per cent business rates retention scheme when this measure was previously considered by Government. The Government should repeat this approach.
Given that increased business rates retention is the only significant financial offer to councils in the Budget, we would urge Government to move at pace on this measure rather than following the proposed timetable of the “end of the decade”. In particular, it is essential that councils have clarity on the process of replacing grants with retained business rates, and the likely grants in scope.

The LGA welcomes the proposal to introduce a General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR) for business rates in England. We have long called for a GAAR as part of a broader crack down on business rates avoidance. We look forward to seeing the consultation, and the implementation of the measure, as soon as possible and want to work with the Government so councils can tackle abuses and avoidance of business rates and ensure that the rules on reliefs such as empty property and charitable relief are applied fairly
The LGA responded to the Government’s call for evidence on Business Rates and Investment and we look forward to seeing the Government’s response.
The government is increasing the relief for pubs, social clubs and all but the very largest live music venues in England by 20ppt, from 15 per cent to 35 per cent from 1 April 2027. The very largest live music venues (with a rateable value of £1 million or above) will not receive this increased rate of relief, but will continue to benefit from the previously announced 15 per cent relief in 2026-27 and real-term freeze in 2027-28 and 2028-29, as announced in January 2026. This will provide ongoing support to qualifying properties, with the level kept under review alongside the 2029 revaluation. (Page 130, paragraph 6.189)

The government is increasing the Small Business Rates Relief (SBRR) eligibility thresholds for qualifying Retail, Hospitality and Leisure (RHL) properties in England from 1 April 2027. The threshold for 100 per cent relief will increase to a rateable value of £18,000, and the threshold for tapered relief will increase to a rateable value of £21,000. These thresholds will provide ongoing support to qualifying properties, with their level kept under review alongside the 2029 revaluation. (Page 130, paragraph 6.190)

From April 2027, Adult Gaming Centres in England will no longer be eligible for the retail, hospitality, and leisure (RHL) multipliers, and vape shops in England will no longer be eligible for the RHL multipliers and the Small Business Rates Relief. (Page 130, paragraph 6.195)

The LGA welcomes business rates reliefs as they will provide support to a range of businesses. However, we believe councils should have greater flexibility to tailor reliefs locally.
Specifically, we urge the Government to provide councils with more flexibility on business rates reliefs such as charitable and empty property relief.
Additionally, we will be seeking assurances from Government in the coming days that councils will be fully compensated for any centrally-mandated reliefs and provided with adequate funding for administrative and IT burdens that might be incurred through their implementation. Account also needs to be taken of the consequences for business rates retention and sufficient time needs to be given for implementation.
Removing vape shops from the RHL multipliers and Small Business Rates Relief needs a definition set out in regulations. That definition should use the existing "wholly or mainly" test and link to the retail licensing scheme under the Tobacco and Vapes Act, so eligibility follows one verifiable register. Businesses that trade mainly in vaping products should not keep relief through reclassification or minor changes to stock. Councils will face new costs from classification reviews, appeals and avoidance, and these should be fully funded as a new burden.

HVCTS applies to England only and this measure will be introduced through Finance Bill 2026-27. (Page 134, paragraph 6.234)
